strategies.name: Find the conclusion first
strategies.summary: Locate the claim everything else is offered to support, then the support. Every LR task is defined relative to that conclusion.

strategies.name: Name the gap
strategies.summary: Write the premise terms and the conclusion terms side by side. The new term in the conclusion is where the argument leaps, and where the answer lives.

strategies.name: Negation test
strategies.summary: Negate a candidate answer. If the argument falls apart without it, it was necessary; if the argument survives, it was not.

strategies.name: Bridge the terms
strategies.summary: Build the conditional that carries the premise term to the conclusion term. The answer that guarantees the conclusion is the bridge, stated in the right direction.

strategies.name: Pre-phrase the answer
strategies.summary: Say what the right answer must do before reading a single choice, so the choices are checked against your prediction rather than each other.

strategies.name: Diagram the conditionals
strategies.summary: Symbolise every if-then, take its contrapositive, and chain them. Converse and inverse readings are the distractors, and the diagram makes them visible.

strategies.name: Abstract the form
strategies.summary: Strip the content and keep the skeleton: quantifiers, direction, validity. Match skeletons, never topics.

strategies.name: Name the flaw in your own words
strategies.summary: Before reading the choices, say what went wrong between premise and conclusion. Then find the choice that says the same thing in the test's abstract vocabulary.

strategies.name: Attack or defend the link
strategies.summary: The premises are given as true. Strengthen or weaken the inference from them to the conclusion, never the premises themselves.

strategies.name: Keep both facts true
strategies.summary: The credited answer lets both surprising findings stand at once. Anything that denies one side or explains only one side is a distractor.

strategies.name: Variance test
strategies.summary: Answer the candidate question both ways. If one answer strengthens and the other weakens, the question is useful; if the argument is untouched either way, it is not.

strategies.name: Stay inside the text
strategies.summary: An inference must be provable from what is written. Prefer the most modest choice; a choice that needs outside knowledge or a stronger word than the text used is wrong.

strategies.name: Test every condition
strategies.summary: Split the principle into its trigger conditions and check each choice against all of them. A scenario that meets most of the conditions meets none of the principle.

strategies.name: Two-speaker test
strategies.summary: For a point at issue, both speakers must address the claim and take opposite sides. One silent speaker or two speakers who agree fails the test.

strategies.name: Map the passage
strategies.summary: Note each paragraph's job and the author's stance as you read. Global questions are answered from the map, not from rereading.

strategies.name: Locate, then verify
strategies.summary: Find the lines the question points at and match the choice against them word for word. Passage vocabulary recombined into an unstated claim is the standard distractor.

strategies.name: Calibrate the tone
strategies.summary: Match the hedging in the author's own words. 'Qualified approval' and 'unqualified enthusiasm' differ by exactly the words the passage used.

strategies.name: Role, not content
strategies.summary: Ask why the author put the reference there, not what it says. The answer names its argumentative job: illustrate, concede, rebut, qualify.

strategies.name: Check both passages
strategies.summary: A comparative answer must be supportable from each passage. Confirm it against both texts, not just the one that comes to mind.

strategies.name: Let context fix the meaning
strategies.summary: Reread the sentence before and after the quoted phrase. The author's contrast pins the local sense, and the dictionary sense is the trap.

strategies.name: Build the board first
strategies.summary: Set up the slots, symbolise every rule, and make the up-front deductions before touching a question. Time spent here is repaid on every question after.

strategies.name: Rule-by-rule elimination
strategies.summary: Take one rule at a time and strike every choice that breaks it. Four wrong answers each violate a different rule, so you never have to build anything.

strategies.name: Apply the new condition
strategies.summary: Write the question's 'if' onto a fresh copy of the board and chain the inferences it forces. Answer from the mini-board, not from memory.

strategies.name: Hunt for a counterexample
strategies.summary: For a global must-be-true, a choice that fails in even one valid arrangement is out. Use earlier acceptable arrangements as ready-made counterexamples.

strategies.name: Witness and contradiction
strategies.summary: Prove the credited number with one arrangement that achieves it, then show one more (or one fewer) breaks a rule. Both halves are required.

strategies.name: Enumerate the distributions
strategies.summary: List every legal split of counts across the groups before placing anyone. The list is the whole answer to a numeric question.

strategies.name: Check both directions
strategies.summary: A substitute rule must forbid everything the original forbade and permit everything it permitted. Test each choice in both directions.

strategies.name: Chain the contrapositives
strategies.summary: Every membership rule has a contrapositive; write them all and follow the chain from the given element. The chain is the deduction.

strategies.name: Track both dimensions
strategies.summary: In a hybrid game every inference must be checked against order and group together. A deduction that ignores one dimension is a guess.

traps.name: The opposite answer
traps.summary: Does the reverse of what the stem asked: a weakener on a strengthen question, a sufficient condition on a necessary one.

traps.name: Too strong
traps.summary: Says 'all', 'never', 'proves' where the text only said 'some', 'usually', 'suggests'. Extra strength is extra claims you cannot support.

traps.name: Too narrow
traps.summary: True of one paragraph or one premise, but not of the whole argument or passage the stem asked about.

traps.name: Out of scope
traps.summary: Introduces a term, party or concern the stimulus never addresses. Plausible in the world, irrelevant to the argument.

traps.name: Premise booster
traps.summary: Restates or shores up a premise instead of bridging premise to conclusion. The premises were already granted.

traps.name: Reversed conditional
traps.summary: The converse or inverse of a rule: 'if Q then P' offered for 'if P then Q'. Only the contrapositive is equivalent.

traps.name: Wrong term
traps.summary: Correctly alleges a shift in meaning, but in a term the argument used consistently.

traps.name: A flaw the argument did not commit
traps.summary: Names a real, well-known error (ad hominem, sampling, circularity) that this particular argument never made.

traps.name: True of the argument, but not a defect
traps.summary: Accurately describes something the argument did, without that thing being a mistake.

traps.name: Sample size red herring
traps.summary: Complains the sample was small when the real problem is how it was selected. Size is rarely the tested defect.

traps.name: Same topic, different structure
traps.summary: Matches the stimulus on subject matter and diverges on form. Parallel and analogy questions are decided on form alone.

traps.name: Dictionary sense
traps.summary: The ordinary meaning of the quoted phrase rather than the meaning the author's contrast fixed for it.

traps.name: Supported by one passage only
traps.summary: True of Passage A or Passage B alone, offered as a claim about both, or attributes one author's view to the other.

traps.name: Polarity flip
traps.summary: The right topic with the wrong sign: approval read as criticism, or the author's opponent's view read as the author's.

traps.name: Intensity overshoot
traps.summary: Right direction, wrong strength: 'hostile' for 'skeptical', 'unqualified' for 'cautious'.

traps.name: Half the paradox
traps.summary: Explains why one finding happened without saying why the other did too, or simply denies one of them.

traps.name: Equivalent in one direction only
traps.summary: A substitute rule that permits nothing new but forbids something old, or the reverse. Equivalence needs both.

traps.name: True of most boards
traps.summary: Holds in most valid arrangements but not all. A single counterexample arrangement kills a must-be-true answer.

traps.name: Answered a different question
traps.summary: A could-be-true offered where must-be-true was asked, or the EXCEPT overlooked so four right answers look wrong.

traps.name: Achievable in isolation
traps.summary: A count or placement that works on its own but collides with another rule once the rest of the board is filled.

traps.name: Quantifier swap
traps.summary: 'Most' where the text said 'some', 'all' where it said 'most'. A single quantifier word changes what follows.

traps.name: Concession mistaken for conclusion
traps.summary: Picks the clause the author granted to the other side, or a premise sitting behind 'since', as the main conclusion.

cues: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
Which one of the following can be properly concluded on the basis of the statements above?
playbooks.task: Apply the given conditionals forward: a rule plus a fact that triggers it yields what must be true.
method: Symbolise each conditional as an arrow and note which fact triggers which rule.
Chain the triggered rules forward to their consequences.
The credited answer is a consequence of the chain; check it appears on the diagram.
Reject anything that runs the arrow backwards or adds a hedge the rules do not contain.

cues: Which one of the following can be properly concluded from the statements above?
If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
playbooks.task: A rule plus the denial of its consequence yields the denial of its trigger.
method: Write the rule as an arrow and immediately write its contrapositive beneath it.
Find the fact that negates the rule's consequent.
Read the contrapositive forward: the trigger is denied.
Any choice that affirms the consequent or denies the antecedent is the converse or inverse in disguise.

cues: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
Which one of the following must be true?
playbooks.task: Find the one claim the statements strictly entail, with no new information added.
method: Treat every statement as true and list what they jointly force.
Combine two statements that share a term; the overlap is where entailments hide.
Prefer the most modest choice that the statements guarantee.
Reject choices that are merely likely, that strengthen a statement, or that swap a quantifier.

cues: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?
playbooks.task: Pick the claim the findings favour most, which will be the weakest choice that still follows.
method: Note what the findings jointly point toward without quite proving.
Predict a hedged claim: 'at least some', 'may', 'probably'.
Choose the choice that stays closest to that hedge.
Strike anything that says 'proves' or 'all', and anything that is true in the world but not in the passage.

cues: If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?
playbooks.task: Find the one choice that contradicts the statements; the other four are each consistent with them.
method: Write the constraints: conditionals, quantifiers, counts.
For each choice, ask which constraint it would violate.
Exactly one collides; name the constraint it hits.
Do not eliminate a choice for being unlikely, only for being impossible.

cues: Which one of the following is the main conclusion of the argument?
Which one of the following most accurately expresses the conclusion drawn in the argument?
playbooks.task: Identify the claim everything else supports, which is often buried mid-paragraph behind a 'since' or a concession.
method: Apply the 'because' test: X because Y means X is the conclusion.
Watch for a concession ('although', 'admittedly') and set it aside; it is not the point.
Paraphrase the conclusion in your own words before reading the choices.
Match the paraphrase; the credited answer restates, it does not extend.

cues: The claim that ... plays which one of the following roles in the argument?
cue_patterns: plays which one of the following roles
playbooks.task: Say what job the quoted claim does: premise, intermediate conclusion, main conclusion, or concession.
method: Find the main conclusion first; every other role is defined relative to it.
Ask of the quoted claim: is it supported by something, and does it support something?
Supported and supporting means intermediate conclusion; supporting only means premise.
The credited answer names the role abstractly; choices that describe content instead of role are decoys.

cues: The argument proceeds by
The colleague responds to the claim by
The argument does which one of the following?
cue_patterns: does which one of the following
playbooks.task: Describe the technique the argument uses, abstractly, without judging whether it works.
method: Name the move in plain words: gives a counterexample, draws an analogy, rules out alternatives, reduces to absurdity.
Translate to the test's abstract vocabulary before reading choices.
Check every part of the credited description actually happened in the argument.
A choice that describes a technique used in a nearby argument type, but not here, is the standard distractor.

cues: Halvorsen and Diaz disagree over whether
playbooks.task: Find the one proposition both speakers address and take opposite positions on.
method: Summarise each speaker's conclusion in one line.
For each choice, ask: does speaker one have a view on this? Does speaker two?
Only a choice both have addressed survives; then check they disagree rather than agree.
A choice one speaker never mentions fails, however strongly the other feels about it.

cues: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
playbooks.task: Supply the claim the preceding sentences were built to license, watching whether the blank follows 'therefore' or 'because'.
method: Look at the word before the blank: 'therefore' wants the conclusion, 'because' wants a missing premise.
Predict the sentence from the setup before reading choices.
Pick the choice the earlier sentences were assembled toward.
Topical, true statements that were never built toward are the distractors.

cues: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?
Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
The conclusion depends on which one of the following assumptions?
cue_patterns: depends on (which one of the following )?assum
playbooks.task: Find the unstated claim the argument cannot survive without.
method: Write the conclusion's terms beside the premises' terms and find the new one.
Predict a modest claim that closes the gap.
Negate each contender: the credited answer's negation wrecks the argument.
A choice that would help enormously but whose negation leaves the argument standing is not necessary.

cues: Which one of the following, if assumed, allows the conclusion above to be properly drawn?
The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
playbooks.task: Find the claim that, added to the premises, guarantees the conclusion.
method: Diagram the premises and the conclusion; note the term the premises reach and the term the conclusion needs.
Write the bridge: if (premise term) then (conclusion term).
Choose the choice that states that bridge, or something stronger.
A bridge in the other direction, or between the wrong terms, is the usual trap.

cues: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
playbooks.task: Pick the new fact that makes the conclusion more likely to follow from the premises.
method: Find the conclusion and the kind of support (causal, sample, analogy).
Ask what would rule out the obvious alternative explanation or confirm the mechanism.
Pick the choice that does that; treat 'if true' as licence to accept it.
Ignore choices about cost, popularity or authority; they do not touch the inference.

cues: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
playbooks.task: Pick the new fact that makes the conclusion less likely to follow from the premises.
method: Find the conclusion and the inference it rests on.
Predict the attack: a confound, reverse causation, a disanalogy, a bad sample.
Choose the choice that supplies it; do not reward a choice that merely denies a premise.
A choice that restates the conclusion, or attacks an irrelevance, is a decoy.

cues: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the argument?
playbooks.task: Find the question whose answer would swing the argument one way or the other.
method: Find the unaddressed alternative explanation.
For each choice, answer it yes and then no.
The credited question strengthens with one answer and weakens with the other.
A question whose either answer leaves the argument untouched is not useful, however interesting.

cues: The argument's reasoning is flawed because it
The reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
playbooks.task: The argument saw two things together and concluded one caused the other. Name that leap.
method: Find the causal word in the conclusion: 'causes', 'responsible for', 'leads to'.
Check the premises: they show correlation, timing, or co-occurrence, not mechanism.
Name the missing possibilities: a third factor, reverse causation, coincidence.
Pick the choice that says the argument failed to rule those out.

cues: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
The argument is flawed because it
playbooks.task: Say what went wrong between premise and conclusion, then find that defect in the test's abstract wording.
method: Find the conclusion and the support, then the step that does not follow.
Name the defect in your own words: reversed conditional, part for whole, false choice, hasty leap.
Translate to the test's phrasing: 'takes for granted that', 'infers merely because'.
Verify the credited choice describes something the argument actually did, and that it is a defect.

cues: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
playbooks.task: One key word means one thing in the premise and another in the conclusion. Find the word.
method: Underline the term that appears in both premise and conclusion.
Ask whether it means the same thing in each place: scope, sense, measure.
Name the two senses.
The credited choice pinpoints the shifted term; a choice alleging a shift in a different term is the trap.

cues: The reasoning is flawed because it
The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
playbooks.task: The argument treats absence of proof as proof of absence, or the reverse.
method: Find the phrase 'no evidence', 'has not been shown', 'nobody has proved'.
Check the conclusion: it asserts the opposite is therefore true.
Name it: lack of evidence settles nothing either way.
Choices about sample size, motives, or definitions describe flaws not committed.

cues: The reasoning above is most vulnerable to criticism on the ground that it
playbooks.task: A rate in the premise became a count in the conclusion, or the reverse, while the denominator went unmentioned.
method: Mark every percentage, share, and raw number in the stimulus.
Check whether the conclusion changes the unit.
Ask what the denominator would have to be for the leap to hold.
The credited choice names the confusion; choices about sampling or causation are decoys.

cues: The reasoning is flawed because it
playbooks.task: The group observed was selected in a way that makes it unlike the population concluded about.
method: Find the group observed and the population the conclusion is about.
Ask how the group was gathered: self-selection, survivorship, convenience.
Name the mismatch between how it was gathered and who it is meant to represent.
Do not reach for 'too small'; the tested defect is selection, and size is the planted wrong answer.

cues: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument
playbooks.task: The premise is the conclusion in different words.
method: Paraphrase the conclusion and each premise in the plainest words you can.
If one premise now reads the same as the conclusion, the support is circular.
Name it: the argument presupposes what it sets out to establish.
Choices describing merely weak support or an unstated assumption describe a different defect.

cues: The argument above is most similar in its reasoning to which one of the following?
The pattern of reasoning above is most closely paralleled by which one of the following?
playbooks.task: Find the argument with the same logical skeleton, in any subject, with the same validity.
method: Reduce the stimulus to a form: all P are Q; x is P; so x is Q.
Note the conclusion's strength and whether the argument is valid.
Diagram each choice the same way and compare forms, ignoring topic.
One quantifier downgrade, one reversed arrow, or one extra premise breaks the match.

cues: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its flawed reasoning to the argument above?
cue_patterns: flawed in a way most similar
playbooks.task: Find the argument that commits the same formal error, not merely a bad argument.
method: Name the flaw in the stimulus first: affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent, part for whole.
Diagram it so the error is visible as a shape.
Diagram each choice; keep only the one with the identical broken shape.
A choice that is a valid argument on the same topic is planted to be picked on content.

cues: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain this apparent discrepancy?
Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent paradox?
playbooks.task: Supply the fact that lets both surprising findings be true at the same time.
method: State the two findings and the word that makes them clash ('yet', 'nevertheless').
Ask what difference between the two situations would produce both results.
Choose the fact that explains both sides at once.
A choice that deepens the puzzle or accounts for only one finding is a decoy.

cues: Which of the following situations conforms to this principle?
Which one of the following judgements most closely conforms to the principle?
playbooks.task: Find the scenario that satisfies every trigger condition of the stated rule.
method: Split the principle into its conditions and its outcome; note 'only if' and exceptions.
For each choice, check each condition in turn.
Only a scenario meeting all of them conforms.
A scenario meeting most conditions, or tripping an exception, is the planted near miss.

cues: Both passages are committed to which one of the following?
The author of Passage A and the author of Passage B would be most likely to disagree about whether
Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?
playbooks.task: Describe the relationship between the two texts: what both hold, where they part, or how one's approach differs.
method: Before the questions, write one line each: what A argues, what B argues, and the point where they meet.
For each choice, test it against A, then separately against B.
The credited answer survives both tests.
A choice that one passage supports and the other never addresses is the standard distractor.

cues: In using the phrase "...", the author most likely means to convey that
The phrase "..." is used primarily to indicate that
playbooks.task: Say what the quoted phrase means where it sits, which the author's contrast fixes.
method: Find the sentence containing the phrase and read the one before and after it.
Identify the contrast the author is drawing with it.
Restate the phrase in plain words that fit that contrast.
The ordinary dictionary sense, and a sense the phrase carries elsewhere, are the decoys.

cues: ... is most analogous to which one of the following?
Which one of the following would best illustrate the passage's claim that
playbooks.task: Find the scenario that shares the structure of the situation described, in an unrelated domain.
method: Reduce the passage situation to a relationship skeleton: who depends on whom for what.
Discard the subject matter entirely.
Match each choice's skeleton to yours.
The choice from the passage's own domain that matches topic and not structure is planted.

cues: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
playbooks.task: Describe the passage as an abstract sequence of moves, in the order they occur.
method: Write one verb per paragraph: introduces, criticises, qualifies, proposes.
Check each choice's sequence against your map, in order.
The credited answer matches every move and adds none.
A choice that imports a move that never happened, or permutes the order, is wrong.

cues: The author mentions X primarily in order to
The primary function of the fourth paragraph is to
The discussion of X functions primarily to
playbooks.task: Say why the author included the reference: the job it does for the argument.
method: Find the reference and read the sentences around it.
Ask what claim it serves: illustrating, conceding, rebutting, qualifying.
Pick the choice naming that role.
A choice that describes what the reference says, or assigns a role to a claim the passage never makes, is wrong.

cues: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
cue_patterns: passage as a whole is primarily
playbooks.task: State the claim the whole passage exists to make, including the author's stance.
method: From your paragraph map, say the passage's point in one sentence before reading choices.
Check that the credited answer covers the whole arc, not one paragraph.
Check it carries the author's attitude, not just the topic.
Strike choices that overstate, or that contradict a qualification the author made.

cues: The author's attitude toward X is best described as
The author's assessment of X is best characterized as
playbooks.task: Name the author's stance toward a specific target, calibrated to the passage's hedging.
method: Find every evaluative word the author uses about the target.
Decide the direction (approves, doubts) and the strength (cautious, wholehearted).
Pick the choice matching both direction and strength.
Polarity flips and intensity overshoots are the two families of wrong answer.

cues: According to the passage, ...
cue_patterns: which one of the following is (true|mentioned|cited) in the passage
playbooks.task: Find the fact the passage states and match the choice that paraphrases it.
method: Use the stem's keywords to find the line.
Read the sentence in full, including any qualifier.
Match the choice against the sentence, term for term.
Passage vocabulary recombined into an unstated claim, or the right fact about the wrong entity, is the trap.

cues: It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that
The passage most strongly supports which one of the following?
The author would be most likely to regard
playbooks.task: Find the claim that follows from combining what the passage says, with nothing added.
method: Find the two or three sentences the question draws on.
Combine them; the inference is what they jointly imply.
Prefer the most modest choice they support.
Real-world plausibility is not support; a hedged passage claim restated as certainty is wrong.

cues: Which one of the following, if substituted for the rule that ..., would have the same effect in determining the order?
playbooks.task: Find the replacement rule that leaves the set of valid arrangements exactly unchanged.
method: Write what the original rule forbids and what it permits.
For each choice, ask: does it forbid anything the original allowed? Does it allow anything the original forbade?
Only a choice answering no to both is equivalent.
Each distractor fails in exactly one direction; that too-strong or too-weak split is the lesson.

cues: What is the greatest number of essays that could be selected?
What is the maximum number of presentations that can be given in the Belfry?
playbooks.task: Find the largest or smallest count that satisfies every rule at once.
method: Start from the extreme the question asks for and try to build one arrangement achieving it.
If it builds, that is your witness; if not, step one toward the middle and retry.
Then show that one more (or one fewer) breaks a rule.
A count achievable on its own but blocked once the rest of the board fills is the trap.

cues: Which one of the following could be an accurate list of the number of clients assigned to each attorney, respectively?
playbooks.task: Work out the legal splits of counts across the groups before placing anyone.
method: Write the total and each group's bounds.
List every distribution of counts that respects the bounds.
Strike distributions any rule excludes.
Answer from the surviving list; distributions the rules exclude are the distractors.

cues: Which one of the following could be the order in which the associates argue, from first to fifth?
Which one of the following could be a complete and accurate list of the essays selected?
playbooks.task: Find the one arrangement that breaks no rule, by striking each choice that breaks one.
method: Take the first rule and strike every choice that violates it.
Repeat with each rule in turn.
One choice survives; that is the answer, and you built nothing.
Do not test choices against the whole board; the rules are the faster filter.

cues: Each of the following could be true EXCEPT:
Which one of the following CANNOT be true?
playbooks.task: Four choices are each possible in some valid arrangement; find the one that is impossible.
method: Read the stem twice; the EXCEPT or CANNOT inverts what you are looking for.
For each choice, try to build one arrangement making it true.
A choice you can build is eliminated.
The choice that collides with a rule every time is the answer; derive the contradiction to be sure.

cues: If H argues third, then which one of the following must be true?
playbooks.task: Add the question's new condition to the board and follow the chain of inferences it forces.
method: Copy the board and write the 'if' onto it.
Chain the deductions the condition forces, two or three steps deep.
Answer from the mini-board.
The condition holds for this question only; do not carry it to the next.

cues: Which one of the following must be true? (in a selection game)
playbooks.task: A global question in a selection game: chain the membership rules and their contrapositives.
method: Write every membership rule with its contrapositive.
Follow the chain from any forced element.
Check the numerical constraint on how many are in and out.
A choice that affirms a consequent or drops a negation breaks one link of the chain.

cues: Which one of the following must be true? (in a game combining order and group)
playbooks.task: A global question in a game with two actions: order and group. Every inference must respect both.
method: Draw a board with both dimensions visible: slots for order, marks for group.
Apply ordering rules and grouping rules to the same board.
For each choice, look for a valid board where it fails.
A deduction made from one dimension alone is the standard mistake.

cues: Which one of the following must be true? (in a grouping game)
playbooks.task: A global question in a grouping game: the answer follows from chaining the conditional membership rules.
method: Write each 'if J then not K' rule and its contrapositive.
Note which elements are forced together or apart.
For each choice, hunt for a valid grouping that breaks it.
Only the choice with no counterexample must be true.

cues: Which one of the following must be true?
Which one of the following could be true?
playbooks.task: With no new condition, find what holds across every valid arrangement (or, for could-be-true, in at least one).
method: Use the deductions you made when building the board; a global answer is usually one of them.
For a must-be-true, try to break each choice with a valid arrangement, reusing earlier acceptable orders.
For a could-be-true, build one arrangement where the choice holds.
A choice that is true in most arrangements but not all is the planted wrong answer.
